name: DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol)

card.summary: An industrial mitochondrial uncoupler that burns fat as heat, banned for human use since 1938 and tied to documented deaths.
card.note: No antidote exists; overdose causes fatal hyperthermia, and UK regulators classify it as a poison.

quick.overview:
DNP is an industrial chemical that was sold as a diet drug in the 1930s and withdrawn after reports of cataracts, blindness and deaths. It has resurfaced online, where bodybuilders and others discussing fast fat loss on looksmaxxing forums describe taking it to cut weight.

Users on forums report rapid weight loss over a few weeks, alongside heat, sweating and fever. Regulators and clinicians describe it as having a narrow gap between effective and toxic exposure.
quick.mechanism: DNP acts as a protonophore: it lets protons leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane, so energy that would have made ATP is released as heat and metabolic rate rises.
quick.risks: Documented harms include dangerously high body temperature, cataracts, nerve damage and death, with no specific antidote. It is banned for human consumption in many countries, prohibited by WADA since 2015, and was reclassified as a regulated poison in the UK in 2023.

lead: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) is an industrial chemical that uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria, converting food energy into heat rather than stored chemical energy. It was marketed as a weight-loss drug in the United States in the 1930s and was judged too toxic for human consumption under the 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.[1]

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities, DNP is discussed as a short-term fat-loss agent for cutting. Users on looksmax.org describe multi-week courses with large reported weight losses, often combined with other substances.[2][3] Clinicians and regulators describe it as having a low therapeutic index and documented fatalities.[1]

No published clinical trial has tested DNP as an appearance or weight-loss treatment in modern times. Evidence about its effects in humans comes mainly from 1930s clinical reports, toxicology and poison-centre case data.[1]
infobox: Dissipates the mitochondrial proton gradient, releasing energy as heat [1]

paras: DNP is a protonophore that shuttles protons across membranes, dissipating the proton gradient that mitochondria use to make ATP. The energy is lost as heat, and metabolic rate rises in a dose-dependent way.[1] Its mechanism was described by Loomis and Lipmann in 1948.[1]

Munitions workers in France during World War I became ill and some died after DNP exposure.[1] In 1933 Maurice Tainter at Stanford reported average weight loss of about 20 pounds in treated patients, and by 1934 he estimated at least 100,000 Americans had been treated, with three reported deaths.[1]

In 1935 the American Medical Association's Council on Chemistry and Pharmacy declined to list the drug, and reports of cataracts emerged. In 1936 a San Francisco ophthalmologist estimated that 2,500 American women had been blinded by it. Some sellers marketed it as a cosmetic to avoid drug regulation.[1] In 1938 the expanded federal law led the FDA to treat DNP as too toxic for human consumption.[1]
Use rose again in the twenty-first century as DNP became available through online sellers, with users including bodybuilders, fitness enthusiasts and people with eating disorders.[1]

Overdose causes hyperthermia that can reach about 44 degrees Celsius, with rapid heart rate, sweating and rapid breathing. Early symptoms include nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain.[1] Reported longer-term harms include cataracts with permanent vision loss, hearing loss, peripheral neuritis and low white-cell counts; animal studies found teratogenic, mutagenic and carcinogenic effects.[1]

There is no antidote, and treatment is supportive, centred on aggressive cooling. Poison-control data from 2010 to 2020 showed an 11.9 percent fatality rate among reported cases, and at least 50 overdose deaths were reported worldwide in that period; deaths in overdose cases have occurred within hours.[1]

DNP is banned for human consumption in many countries, although it remains legal to sell for non-human uses in many jurisdictions. WADA has prohibited it since 2015, and Interpol and WADA issued an orange notice about its dangers that year.[1] In 2018 a UK seller was convicted of manslaughter for supplying DNP for human consumption, and was convicted of gross negligence manslaughter after a 2020 retrial. The UK made DNP a regulated poison in October 2023.[1]

Looksmax.org contains many threads in which members log DNP courses, ask where to obtain it and compare it with other fat-loss approaches.[2][3] Posters report heat, fever and fatigue early in use, and some report large weight losses over two to three weeks while eating very little.[3] Some members note that others in the forum have not tried it and have heard it can kill; replies in these threads range from reassurance to caution.[3]

Users also describe combining DNP with GLP-1-type drugs, anabolic steroids and other agents, and some argue that these combinations give better results.[2][4] No studies have examined such combinations.

Researchers disagree about public warnings. One group has advised against awareness campaigns because they might increase interest in the drug, while another has argued that UK campaigns in the early 2010s reduced use.[1]

No modern clinical trials of DNP for weight loss or appearance were found. Historical clinical reports from the 1930s described weight loss alongside serious harms.[1] A related experimental prodrug, HU6, has completed a phase II trial in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which reported reduced liver fat and body weight with no serious adverse effects; it is a different compound from DNP.[1]

timeline.event: Tainter publishes weight-loss results with DNP at Stanford.[1]
AMA council declines to list DNP; cataract reports emerge.[1]
Federal law leads FDA to treat DNP as too toxic for human use.[1]
Loomis and Lipmann describe its uncoupling mechanism.[1]
WADA bans DNP; Interpol and WADA issue a warning notice.[1]
UK reclassifies DNP as a regulated poison.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org DNP appears in cutting logs and sourcing threads, typically discussed as a fast way to lose fat before a target date.[2][3]

claims.claim: DNP produces very fast fat loss over a few weeks.
claims.believers: Posters report losing roughly 20 pounds in about two weeks with minimal exercise while eating very little.[3]
claims.experts: DNP raises metabolic rate by uncoupling mitochondria, and 1930s patients lost weight, but weight loss was accompanied by serious toxicity.[1]

claims.claim: The dangers are manageable with hydration and avoiding hot weather.
claims.believers: Some forum members say it is not that bad if users stay hydrated and avoid summer heat.[3]
claims.experts: Toxicologists describe a low therapeutic index, no antidote and an 11.9 percent fatality rate in poison-centre cases from 2010 to 2020.[1]

claims.claim: DNP stacked with GLP-1 drugs, testosterone or other agents is an efficient cutting combination.
claims.believers: Members describe pairing DNP with retatrutide, testosterone and diet protocols and say the combination outperforms DNP alone.[2][4]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined these combinations.

claims.believers: Some posters claim that very large single ingestions are survivable based on personal experience.[2]
claims.experts: Published case data report fatalities at ingested amounts as low as 4.3 mg/kg and typical fatal overdoses at 20 to 50 mg/kg, with symptoms beginning within hours.[1]
